questions.q: Write the complex number \( \sqrt{-25} \) in standard form \( a + ib \) and state its real and imaginary parts.
questions.a: The standard form is \( 0 + 5i \). Real part \( = 0 \), Imaginary part \( = 5 \). A wrong answer like \( 5i \) without the zero real part, or stating the imaginary part as \( 5i \) instead of \( 5 \), reveals confusion between the imaginary part (a real number) and the imaginary component (which includes \( i \)).

questions.q: If \( z = 3 - 4i \), what are \( \text{Re}(z) \) and \( \text{Im}(z) \)? A student says \( \text{Im}(z) = -4i \). Explain why this is incorrect.
questions.a: \( \text{Re}(z) = 3 \), \( \text{Im}(z) = -4 \). The imaginary part is defined as the real coefficient of \( i \), not the term \( -4i \). The student’s error shows they conflate the imaginary part with the imaginary term; they need to recall the precise definition: if \( z = a + ib \), then \( \text{Im}(z) = b \) (a real number).

questions.q: Express \( \frac{2 + \sqrt{-16}}{2} \) in standard form \( a + ib \).
questions.a: \( \sqrt{-16} = 4i \). Then \( \frac{2 + 4i}{2} = 1 + 2i \). So \( a = 1, b = 2 \). A wrong answer like \( 1 + 4i \) (forgetting to divide the imaginary part) or \( 1 + 2 \) (treating \( i \) as 1) indicates a procedural gap in simplifying complex expressions.

questions.q: Compare the complex numbers \( z_1 = 5 + 0i \) and \( z_2 = 0 + 5i \). How do their positions on the complex plane differ? (You may describe without drawing.)
questions.a: \( z_1 = 5 \) lies on the real axis (5 units to the right of the origin). \( z_2 = 5i \) lies on the imaginary axis (5 units above the origin). A student who says both are the same or both lie on the real axis has not grasped the geometric distinction between real and imaginary components.

questions.q: A student solves \( x^2 + 9 = 0 \) and writes \( x = \pm 3 \). Evaluate this solution and explain the error.
questions.a: The solution is incorrect because \( (\pm 3)^2 = 9 \), not \( -9 \). The correct solutions are \( x = \pm 3i \). The error stems from ignoring the negative sign under the square root and not introducing \( i \). This reveals a fundamental misunderstanding that the square root of a negative number is not a real number.

questions.q: Create a quadratic equation with real coefficients that has the complex number \( 2 - 3i \) as one of its roots. Write the equation in standard form \( ax^2 + bx + c = 0 \).
questions.a: Since coefficients are real, complex roots occur in conjugate pairs. The other root is \( 2 + 3i \). Sum of roots = 4, product = \( (2)^2 + (3)^2 = 13 \). The equation is \( x^2 - 4x + 13 = 0 \). A poor answer might give an equation with complex coefficients or only one root, showing lack of understanding of the conjugate root theorem for real polynomials.
